title: Civil Services Reform

cards.b: India's civil services run policy delivery from block to Centre. Reform of recruitment, training and accountability is a perennial question across Paper I, GS II and GS IV. Know the committees and the recent moves: lateral entry and Mission Karmayogi.

• Art. 308-314: services of the Union and States; Art. 311 protects against dismissal without inquiry.
  • Art. 312: All-India Services (IAS, IPS, IFoS) by Rajya Sabha resolution.
  • Art. 315-323: UPSC and State PSCs.

Sardar Patel is called the patron saint of the All-India Services. The 'steel frame' phrase is from Lloyd George (1922).

Chaired first by Veerappa Moily. It stressed ethics in governance, performance management, fixed tenures, curbing political interference, lateral entry, and e-governance. It proposed a Civil Services Authority and a restructured Section 311. Many recommendations are still pending.

Problems: frequent transfers, political pressure, lack of specialisation, corruption, weak performance appraisal. T.S.R. Subramanian v Union of India (2013) directed fixed tenure and Civil Services Boards for transfers. Prakash Singh (2006) did similar for the police. Tools: Lokpal and Lokayukta Act (2013), RTI (2005), Citizens' Charter (1997), 360-degree appraisal.

The Government sought specialists at joint secretary and director level from outside the service. The first call was in June 2018 (10 posts), and appointments began in 2019 (the 2017 NITI Aayog proposal). In August 2024, a 45-post advertisement was withdrawn after concerns that reservation was missing. Supporters: expertise, fresh ideas. Critics: reservation, politicisation, and undermining the career bureaucracy.

Launched in September 2020 as the National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building. Its platform, iGOT Karmayogi, offers online learning; competency frameworks aim to move from 'rule-based' to 'role-based' training. A Capacity Building Commission oversees it. It is the main recent reform to know.

Fulton Report (UK, 1968) criticised generalists. India's IAS model is generalist, a 'jack of all trades'. Weber's ideal bureaucracy: rule-bound, neutral and merit-based. Others: development administration (Riggs) stresses attitude change. Challenges: politicians versus 'committed bureaucracy', and cadre allocation, plus the 'permanent versus political executive' tension.

Priorities: merit-based and transparent selection, specialised mid-career tracks, tenure security, performance-linked promotion, digital delivery, and ethical training. Also reforms of State PSCs (paper leaks) and the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024.
